{
  "winner": "A",
  "reasons": [
    "Idea A's payer already pays for this category. Therapists pay incumbents $49–$99/mo (sourced SimplePractice and TherapyNotes pricing pages). Idea B has no evidence that anyone pays for a bot or AI-content filter.",
    "A's demand evidence is about price, a lever a cheaper product can pull. Sourced Reddit threads call SimplePractice 'overkill' and its pricing 'criminal', and the oasys.health interviews say it is 'really expensive for what it offers.' B's demand quotes show annoyance with bots, not intent to buy a tool.",
    "B faces at least four free, actively maintained competitors, some open source, for the same use case. That leaves a paid tier almost no room. A's competitors are expensive, so a $29–$69 product has a plausible price wedge.",
    "The 90-day goal needs one paying customer, not scale. One private-pay solo therapist at about $29–$69/mo is a more reachable conversion than getting a user to pay $1.99/mo when free alternatives exist.",
    "A's main risk is HIPAA/BAA overhead, estimated at $8k–$25k in year one. That is a real cost, but it is a known, budgetable hurdle. B's risks have no clear fix: noisy detection that misflags real users, dependence on third-party page structure, and no demonstrated willingness to pay."
  ],
  "weakest_evidence_in_loser": "B's whole payer hypothesis rests on ReviewGuard's listed $1.99/month Pro price. A listed price is not evidence that anyone pays it. The brief admits no competitor publishes install or revenue numbers, and it offers no evidence that a single user has paid for this kind of extension.",
  "confidence_note": "Moderate. Both briefs argue strongly against their own ideas. A could still fail on HIPAA cost and timeline for a one-person build, and its brief notes that switching interest flows toward full EHRs, not stripped-down tools. A wins mainly because it shows an existing paying buyer and a price gap, while B shows neither."
}
